## Multi-token Prediction as a Training Objective {#sec-ch2}

*Predicting Further Ahead, Without Changing What You Serve*

### Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- Write the standard next-token training objective, then generalize it
  to a multi-token prediction (MTP) objective, and state exactly what
  changes and what stays fixed between the two.
- Distinguish two verified MTP designs — independent parallel heads and
  a sequential causal chain — by what each head/module's input actually
  contains, not just by how many extra outputs each produces.
- Compute the shifted target positions and the total number of
  individual loss terms an MTP objective introduces, given a sequence
  length and a prediction horizon.
- State what is shared versus duplicated across an MTP design's extra
  heads or modules.
- Distinguish MTP (a training-time objective) from speculative decoding
  (an inference-time serving technique), and state what about MTP's
  effect on downstream quality or inference speed is and is not
  supported by the verified sources.

### Why this matters

Ordinary next-token training asks a model one question per position:
*what comes immediately next?* Chapter 1 treated the objective itself
as fixed and focused on the data feeding it. This chapter changes the
objective: at each position, the model is additionally asked to guess
further ahead, using the same context it already has. Two independently
verified, materially different implementations of this idea exist —
one used only as an auxiliary training signal, one deployed in a
671B-parameter production model — and conflating them, or conflating
either with the unrelated inference-time technique they are sometimes
paired with, is the single most common way this topic gets taught
incorrectly.

### Mental model or analogy

::: {.callout-note title="Analogy"}
Picture a student reading a mystery novel one page at a time. The
ordinary exercise is: after each page, guess what happens on the very
next page. Multi-token prediction adds extra exercises at the same
point: also guess what happens two pages ahead, and three pages ahead,
using only what you've read so far. When it's actually time to keep
reading (inference), the teacher only ever asks the "next page"
question — the extra guesses were training exercises, not part of the
real task. **Where this breaks down:** in one of this chapter's two
verified designs, the "two pages ahead" guess is not made blind — the
student is first *told* the correct answer to the "next page" question,
then asked to guess two pages ahead *using* that correct answer. That
chained version is a different exercise from three independent guesses
made all at once, and the two must not be treated as the same thing.
:::

### Technical core

**Baseline: the standard next-token objective.** Ordinary language-model
training minimizes the cross-entropy loss

$$
L_1 = -\sum_t \log P_\theta(x_{t+1} \mid x_{t:1})
$$ {#eq-next-token}

— maximizing the probability of the single next token $x_{t+1}$ given
the history $x_{t:1}$ [@src-43]. Nothing about this chapter changes
@eq-next-token as the model's inference-time behavior; MTP only adds
extra terms during training.

**Generalizing to $n$ future tokens.** Gloeckle et al. generalize
@eq-next-token to predicting $n$ future tokens at once from each
position:

$$
L_n = -\sum_t \log P_\theta(x_{t+n:t+1} \mid x_{t:1})
$$ {#eq-mtp-joint}

which they factorize, under the assumption that a **shared trunk**
produces one latent representation $z_{t:1}$ from which all $n$ future
tokens are predicted **independently of each other**:

$$
L_n = -\sum_t \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log P_\theta(x_{t+i} \mid z_{t:1}) \cdot P_\theta(z_{t:1} \mid x_{t:1})
$$ {#eq-mtp-factorized}

[@src-43]. Concretely, the architecture is a shared trunk $f_s$, $n$
**independent** output heads $f_{h_i}$ (each its own set of transformer
layers), and a **shared** unembedding matrix $f_u$:

$$
P_\theta(x_{t+i} \mid x_{t:1}) = \mathrm{softmax}\bigl(f_u(f_{h_i}(f_s(x_{t:1})))\bigr), \quad i = 1, \ldots, n
$$ {#eq-mtp-heads}

where $P_\theta(x_{t+1} \mid x_{t:1})$ is the ordinary next-token head
[@src-43]. **What is shared versus duplicated:** the trunk $f_s$ and
the unembedding matrix $f_u$ are shared across all $n$ heads; only each
head's own transformer layers $f_{h_i}$ are duplicated per head — the
paper's own contribution is a memory-efficient implementation that
computes each head's forward/backward pass sequentially, discarding
each head's logits before starting the next, which reduces peak GPU
memory from $O(nV+d)$ to $O(V+d)$ ($V$ = vocabulary size, $d$ = latent
dimension) "at no expense in runtime" [@src-43] — the paper's own
stated qualification, not a universal guarantee for every
implementation.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"More prediction heads means proportionally more training compute."**
Per the paper's own memory-accounting argument, the added *parameter*
cost is real (one extra transformer-layer stack per head), but the
paper reports "no train time or memory overhead" for their specific
sequential-computation implementation [@src-43] — this is the source's
own reported result for its own implementation, not a property that
follows automatically from the objective itself in every
implementation.
:::

**A different design: the sequential causal chain (DeepSeek-V3).**
DeepSeek-V3 also adopts an MTP objective, explicitly citing Gloeckle et
al. as its inspiration, but implements it differently: "different from
Gloeckle et al. (2024), which parallelly predicts $D$ additional tokens
using independent output heads, we sequentially predict additional
tokens and keep the complete causal chain at each prediction depth"
[@src-33]. Concretely, depth $k$'s module combines the **previous
depth's** hidden state $h_i^{k-1}$ with the **actual embedding of the
ground-truth token** $t_{i+k}$ (teacher forcing, not the model's own
guess):

$$
h_i'^{\,k} = M_k\bigl[\mathrm{RMSNorm}(h_i^{k-1}); \mathrm{RMSNorm}(\mathrm{Emb}(t_{i+k}))\bigr]
$$ {#eq-mtp-chain-input}

feeds this into depth $k$'s own transformer block to get $h_i^k$, and
predicts the $k$-th additional token with a shared output head
[@src-33]. **What is shared versus duplicated here:** the embedding
layer and the output head are shared across *every* depth *and* with
the main model itself — DeepSeek-V3's own stated design principle
[@src-33] — while each depth's transformer block $\mathrm{TRM}_k$ and
projection matrix $M_k$ are depth-specific. This is a materially
different sharing pattern from the independent-heads design, where the
per-head transformer layers are never shared with each other.

The per-depth loss is a cross-entropy over that depth's valid target
range, and the total MTP loss averages across depths with a single
scalar weight $\lambda$:

$$
L_{\mathrm{MTP}} = \frac{\lambda}{D} \sum_{k=1}^{D} L_{\mathrm{MTP}}^{k}
$$ {#eq-mtp-chain-total}

added as an auxiliary term alongside the main next-token loss
[@src-33].

**Inference-time default, for both designs.** Both papers state the
same default: the auxiliary heads/modules exist only to improve
training, and are discarded at inference, leaving the ordinary
next-token path to "function independently and normally" [@src-33];
Gloeckle et al. state the identical default explicitly [@src-43].

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"MTP is a way of doing speculative decoding."** It is not — MTP is
a *training-time objective*. Both verified sources note, as a
*separate, optional* possibility, that the discarded heads/modules
*could* instead be repurposed as a draft source for speculative
decoding — Gloeckle et al. report up to 3× inference speedup this way
using self-speculative decoding [@src-43]; DeepSeek-V3 states the same
option [@src-33] — but repurposing for speculative decoding is a
distinct design decision, not a consequence of training with MTP. A
model trained with MTP and served with ordinary autoregressive
next-token decoding is common and does not contradict anything in
either paper. Speculative decoding's own acceptance/verification
mechanics are workbook 06's subject, not taught here.
:::

**What is, and is not, supported by these sources.** Both papers report
downstream-capability and/or training-signal-density benefits *for
their own specific models and evaluation suites* — Gloeckle et al.
report their 13B model solving "12% more problems on HumanEval and 17%
more on MBPP" than a comparable next-token model [@src-43]. Neither
paper's result is evidence that MTP universally improves quality for
every model size or task: Gloeckle et al. themselves report that
"multi-token prediction models are worse than the baseline for small
model sizes, but outperform the baseline at scale" [@src-43] — a
model-size-dependent effect, not a universal one. Any specific latency
number attributed to self-speculative decoding is also
implementation- and hardware-dependent, per workbook 04's own general
caution against treating a reported speedup as hardware-independent.

### Worked example

**Target shifting and loss-term counting for a 6-token toy sequence.**
Take the toy sequence $x_1, \ldots, x_6 =$ "The", "cat", "sat", "on",
"the", "mat" ($T = 6$), and a prediction horizon $n = 3$.

**Design 1 (independent heads).** A position $t$ is valid only if
$t + n \le T$ — every head needs a real target token — so $t$ ranges
over $1, 2, 3$ (positions $4, 5, 6$ are excluded: predicting 3 tokens
ahead from position 4 would need a token at position 7, which does not
exist). At each valid $t$, three heads target three different offsets:

| Position $t$ | Context | Head 1 target ($t+1$) | Head 2 target ($t+2$) | Head 3 target ($t+3$) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | "The" | "cat" | "sat" | "on" |
| 2 | "The", "cat" | "sat" | "on" | "the" |
| 3 | "The", "cat", "sat" | "on" | "the" | "mat" |

: Design 1's shifted targets — 3 valid positions x 3 heads = 9 individual loss terms, verified programmatically {#tbl-mtp-design1-targets}

Every one of the $3 \times 3 = 9$ table cells is one term
$-\log P_\theta(x_{t+i} \mid z_{t:1})$ in @eq-mtp-factorized's inner
sum; the combined objective $L_3$ for this toy sequence is the sum of
all 9 terms.

**Design 2 (sequential chain).** For the same toy sequence and depth
$D = 3$, position $i = 1$'s three depths chain as follows:

| Depth $k$ | Input combines | Actual target-token embedding fed in | Predicts |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | main model's hidden state at position 1 | "cat" | "cat" |
| 2 | depth 1's hidden state $h_1^1$ | "sat" | "sat" |
| 3 | depth 2's hidden state $h_1^2$ | "on" | "on" |

: Design 2's chained inputs for position 1 — each depth's input includes the ACTUAL embedding of its own target (teacher forcing), unlike design 1's heads {#tbl-mtp-design2-chain}

Positions $i = 2$ and $i = 3$ chain the same way, shifted by one
position each; design 2 also has exactly $3 \times 3 = 9$ individual
loss terms for this toy sequence, but each depth's *input* — not just
its target — differs structurally from design 1's heads, since depth
$k > 1$'s input already contains the correct answer to depth $k-1$'s
question.

### Compare and contrast

| Aspect | Design 1: independent heads [@src-43] | Design 2: sequential chain [@src-33] |
|---|---|---|
| Head/module input | Shared trunk output $z_{t:1}$ only — identical for every head | Previous depth's hidden state **plus** the actual target-token embedding (teacher forcing) |
| Inter-head dependency | None — heads computed independently | Sequential — depth $k$ depends on depth $k-1$'s output |
| Shared components | Trunk $f_s$, unembedding $f_u$ | Embedding layer, output head (shared across depths **and** with the main model) |
| Duplicated components | Per-head transformer layers $f_{h_i}$ | Per-depth transformer block $\mathrm{TRM}_k$ and projection $M_k$ |
| Loss combination | Flat sum over all $(t, i)$ pairs | Per-depth average, then scaled by one weight $\lambda$ |
| Verified deployment | Auxiliary training signal in the paper's own experiments | Shipped in a 671B-parameter production model |

: Two verified MTP designs compared on structure, not on which is "better" — the sources do not make that comparison against each other {#tbl-mtp-design-comparison}

### Applied exercise

For a sequence of length $T = 10$ and prediction horizon $n = 4$, list
every valid position $t$ for the independent-heads design, write out
each head's target token position (as $t+1, \ldots, t+4$), and confirm
the total number of individual loss terms matches (number of valid
positions) $\times$ (number of heads).

### Interview lens

*"How does multi-token prediction change the training objective, and
does it change what the model does at inference?"* A strong answer
states the generalized objective (@eq-mtp-joint), names at least one
verified design by its actual mechanism (not just "extra heads"), and
explicitly states that both verified designs discard the auxiliary
heads/modules at inference by default — distinguishing this training-
time objective from speculative decoding, which is a separate,
optional, inference-time reuse of the same discarded components. An
answer that says "MTP makes inference faster" without this distinction
is incomplete.

### Chapter recap

- MTP generalizes the standard next-token objective (@eq-next-token) to
  predicting $n$ future tokens per position (@eq-mtp-joint) — an
  addition to training, not a change to inference-time behavior by
  default.
- Two verified designs implement this differently: independent parallel
  heads reading only a shared trunk's output [@src-43], versus a
  sequential causal chain where each depth's input includes the actual
  target embedding of the depth before it [@src-33].
- Each design shares some components (trunk+unembedding, or
  embedding+output-head) and duplicates others (per-head layers, or
  per-depth blocks) — "more heads" is not one undifferentiated cost.
- Both designs discard the auxiliary heads/modules at inference by
  default; repurposing them for self-speculative decoding is a
  separate, optional design decision, not an automatic consequence of
  training with MTP.
- Reported capability gains are specific to each paper's own models and
  benchmarks, and are explicitly model-size-dependent in at least one
  source — not a universal guarantee.

### Sources and further reading

Primary sources for this chapter: [@src-43] (Gloeckle et al., the
independent-heads MTP design, its factorization, and its
memory-efficient implementation — verified via full-text extraction of
the arXiv PDF, Section 2) and [@src-33] (DeepSeek-V3's Section 2.2, the
sequential causal-chain MTP design — verified via full-text extraction
of the same arXiv PDF already registered for workbook 04 chapter 6,
this time read for its MTP section specifically rather than its
architecture case-study content). This chapter deliberately does not
teach speculative decoding's own acceptance/verification mechanics —
that is workbook 06's assigned primary home.
